[[File:Symmetry measure of Reuleaux triangle.svg|thumb|The largest centrally symmetric subset (central shaded region) of a [[Reuleaux triangle]] and its reflection across the center of symmetry of the subset]]
In [[plane geometry]] the '''Kovner–Besicovitch measure''' is a number defined for any bounded [[convex set]] describing how close to being [[central symmetry|centrally symmetric]] it is. It is the fraction of the area of the set that can be covered by its largest centrally symmetric subset.{{r|grunbaum}}

==Properties==
This measure is one for a set that is centrally symmetric, and less than one for sets whose closure is not centrally symmetric. It is invariant under [[affine transformation]]s of the plane. If <math>c</math> is the center of symmetry of the largest centrally-symmetric set within a given convex body <math>K</math>, then the centrally-symmetric set itself is the intersection of <math>K</math> with its reflection across <math>c</math>.{{r|grunbaum}}

==Minimizers==
The convex sets with the smallest possible Kovner–Besicovitch measure are the triangles, for which the measure is 2/3. The result that triangles are the minimizers of this measure is known as '''Kovner's theorem''' or the '''Kovner–Besicovitch theorem''', and the inequality bounding the measure above 2/3 for all convex sets is the '''Kovner–Besicovitch inequality'''.{{r|makaev}}  The [[curve of constant width]] with the smallest possible Kovner–Besicovitch measure is the [[Reuleaux triangle]].{{r|finch}}

==Computational complexity==
The Kovner–Besicovitch measure of any given convex polygon with <math>n</math> vertices can be found in time <math>O(n\log n)</math> by determining a translation of the reflection of the polygon that has the largest possible overlap with the unreflected polygon.{{r|bcdkt}}

==History==
[[Branko Grünbaum]] writes that the Kovner–Besicovitch theorem was first published in Russian, in a 1935 textbook on the [[calculus of variations]] by [[Mikhail Lavrentyev]] and [[Lazar Lyusternik]], where it was credited to Soviet mathematician and geophysicist {{ill|S. S. Kovner|ru|Ковнер, Семён Самсонович}}. Additional proofs were given by [[Abram Samoilovitch Besicovitch]] and by [[István Fáry]], who also proved that every minimizer of the Kovner–Besicovitch measure is a triangle.{{r|grunbaum}}

==See also==
*[[Estermann measure]], a measure of central symmetry defined using supersets in place of subsets
